articles.title: Remembering 9/11, the day that changed everything
articles.summary: 🐘Plus: What you missed at RNC night 2 {beacon} It’s Friday. Let us hold a moment of silence for those who lost their lives 25 years ago. In today’s issue: Former presidents reflect on 9/11 GOP convention Day 2 Trump’s dividend vow faces scrutiny Inflation is steady; gas prices are not Programming note:…
articles.body:
It’s Friday. Let us hold a moment of silence for those who lost their lives 25 years ago.

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Colin Meyn filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

A quarter of a century after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the four living ex-presidents are looking back on the day that reshaped the nation — and the lives of the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York City, Pennsylvania and Virginia.

Former President Clinton said the country can’t erase the pain of 9/11, but it can honor those who were lost by remembering what brought Americans together in the aftermath.

“We can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today,” Clinton wrote . “But we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect, in person and online, and recognizing that what we have in common is far more important than what divides us.”

Former President Obama echoed the sentiment while honoring those who put their lives on the line in the wars that followed.

“Today Michelle and I are remembering those we lost that day, and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed,” Obama said in a statement.

He urged Americans to remember that even “the darkest days” can be overcome “as long as we move forward as one nation and one people.”

Former President George W. Bush , who was in office when the attacks happened, gave remarks earlier this week reflecting on the day and his response as the nation’s leader.

Bush recalled the moment he learned the second World Trade Center tower had been struck while he was visiting an elementary school in Florida.

“I didn’t have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, that my job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country,” he said Wednesday. “And so, it was a moment of clarity.”

Clinton, Obama, Bush and former President Biden participated in the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero in New York City on Friday. They were joined by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , Vice President Vance and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani , among others. 📺 Watch here .

President Trump opted to stay in Washington on Friday, commemorating the day from the Pentagon. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and first lady Melania Trump also attended the memorial ceremony. 👁️ Check it out here .

For many Americans, 9/11 isn’t just a chapter in a history book.

A new Ipsos poll found that 47 percent of adults consider the attacks one of the five most important historic events they’ve lived through. And 75 percent said they personally remember where they were when they learned about the tragedy.

Twenty-five years later, the effects are still visible in everyday life — perhaps nowhere more than at the airport . The attacks ushered in a new era of security screenings, from removing shoes to limits on liquids and tighter restrictions on what travelers can bring through checkpoints.

Some of those rules are now being rolled back under the Trump administration. The Department of Homeland Security, created after the attacks, has eliminated the requirement to remove shoes at Transportation Security Administration (TSA) checkpoints and launched a pilot program allowing non-ticketed passengers through to the gate at some airports. Officials are also considering changes to liquid restrictions for TSA PreCheck passengers.

Those updates reflect advances in screening tech, national security experts say, but also raise questions about how much security is enough.

At the same time, the threat facing the U.S. has changed. The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan launched after 9/11 have ended, while concerns about lone-wolf attacks and other forms of terrorism remain. 👓 Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Bill Sammon here .

And the anniversary comes as the Trump administration has again put the U.S. at the center of conflict in the Middle East, including through the ongoing strikes against Iran.

“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told the crowd at the Pentagon ceremony on Friday.

For a generation of Americans, 9/11 remains a dividing line: the moment the world they knew changed and the beginning of an era whose consequences are still being felt.

For Generation Z, 9/11 isn’t something they remember — it’s something they inherited.

They grew up with airport security, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and the ever-present threat of terrorism as the backdrop to their childhoods.

That may help explain why only 16 percent of Gen Zers say the attacks permanently changed their way of life, compared with 36 percent of millennials. For younger Americans, there may not be one defining tragedy that stands apart from the rest — just a steady stream of crises that have become part of growing up.

Bonus: The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky shares a first-person account of living near Ground Zero.

The first midterm Republican National Committee convention has wrapped, with Vance delivering the closing keynote last night.

Plenty of people in the crowd were ready to crown Vance as the 2028 presidential nominee, though there’s plenty of love for Secretary of State Marco Rubio , too.

The Hill’s Julia Mueller made the trip to Dallas. Read her Night 1 and Night 2 dispatches here.

Here are some notable moments if you weren’t tuned in:

Vance paid an extended tribute to his late friend Charlie Kirk . He noted the conservative activist “hated war,” a view that he conceded was shared by others on the right. “I’m not here to litigate the disagreements between Charlie and some of the people that he disagreed with. What I’m asking you to do is do what Charlie did. Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there,” Vance said.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is drawing criticism from Democrats for a speech in which he tied together the 9/11 attacks and assassination attempts on Trump to what he called a “red-green” alliance between communists and Islamists. As Cruz called out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Senate nominee James Talarico by name, a man in the crowd yelled, “He should be shot,” after each name. Cruz shared a clip here .

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. regaled the audience with a retelling of his jump from Democratic presidential nominee to top Trump surrogate in the 2024 campaign. He criticized the rushed nominating process for former Vice President Kamala Harris and quipped, “The party of ‘No Kings’ anointed a queen!” He said that as Trump wooed him to the Republican campaign, he tried to have a conversation with Harris. “Do you think she would agree to meet with me? Did she even pick up the telephone? No.”

We won’t take it personally: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told the crowd , “It feels better speaking to a stadium full of patriots than a room full of journalists.”

Trump gave remarkably brief remarks after Vance, then enjoyed some pretty amazing opera singing before the night wrapped.

The president reiterated his pledge — announced on Night 1 — that Republicans would cut $5,000 checks to all adults if they maintain power after the midterms.

“If we win the midterms, we will, on the other hand, provide a, let’s call it Trump dividend, $5,000 for every adult citizen in our country, and we can do that because our country has never done better,” he said.

Fiscal hawks in Trump’s party really don’t like this idea.

“Maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) wrote in a post on the social platform X, referring to Trump’s idea.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.), who chaired the House Freedom Caucus, referred to Trump’s dividend as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who’s tried to distance herself from Trump in a tough blue-state reelection race, doesn’t seem hyped on the idea either.

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” Collins said in a statement .

Trump thinks he can move ahead with the proposal without Congress . We’ll find out next week what lawmakers think about that.

Fuel prices have been piling pressure on Americans for months.

Gas prices jumped 3.9 percent in August, while diesel hit a record $6.05 per gallon Friday — up 63 percent from a year ago.

The Iran war, which Trump has acknowledged likely won’t end before the midterms, has added to the pressure, with traffic through the Strait of Hormuz significantly restricted and oil prices climbing above $100 per barrel.

The squeeze goes beyond the pump: Diesel powers the trucks that move much of what Americans buy, meaning higher fuel costs can eventually show up in prices at the store.

Meanwhile, inflation remains stuck at 3.4 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Those numbers leave the Federal Reserve with a tricky decision on interest rates next week.

🧑‍⚖️ Trump ally Joe diGenova resigned from the Department of Justice investigation into alleged schemes against the president, raising new questions about the probe’s direction. DiGenova later said pursuing indictments without evidence would create an “ethical problem.”

🗺️ New Mexico Democrats are pressing Apple and Google to keep the state’s name intact on their navigation apps after the president shared a map labeling it “New America,” arguing he has no authority to rename the Land of Enchantment.

🎥 Hunter Kozak , the man who debated conservative activist Charlie Kirk moments before his assassination, says he has spent the past year facing death threats and conspiracy theories accusing him of involvement in the killing. He says strangers have even confronted him outside his home.

👀 Rubio signaled he has no plans to run for president in 2028, despite speculation that he could be Trump’s GOP successor. “I’m not a candidate for anything right now,” he said.

🚨 Decision Desk HQ’s Senate forecast teetered this week, briefly giving Democrats a 51 percent chance of winning the chamber before swinging back to Republicans on Thursday.

Sunday: Trump holds executive time, attends the Irish Open and then returns to Washington.

🛏️ Celebrate: Today is National Make Your Bed Day. It may be Friday, but like I (Steff) always say, “A made-up bed is a made-up mind to have a good day.”

I (Steff again) was in fourth fourth grade on 9/11. I remember the heartbreak, the chaos, the confusion, the unknown. We wrote letters to the victims’ families in class. It is not something I will ever forget.

articles.title: CIA officer charged in gold bars case working toward a plea deal
articles.summary: A former CIA officer who was arrested this spring with more than 303 gold bars worth $40 million in his home is working to finalize a plea deal with federal prosecutors that could help keep the case shrouded in mystery.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A former CIA officer who was arrested in May after investigators found 303 gold bars worth $40 million at his home is working to finalize a plea deal with federal prosecutors that could help keep the case shrouded in mystery. David Rush and the Justice Department have a “plea agreement in principle,” the parties said Friday, and are asking a judge to extend a forthcoming deadline for the case to be indicted. Rush had only formally been charged with one count of theft of public funds, accused of falsifying pay records in a case that was presented by criminal complaint and has not yet been presented to a federal grand jury. “The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork, including an agreed upon statement of facts,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney Jessica Carmichael wrote in a joint filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.” They are asking for a 21-day extension, through Oct. 8. Judge Leonie Brinkema had previously said there would be no extension past her deadline of Sept. 17. Details of the working plea agreement are not yet available. The case against Rush has brought a spotlight to his relationship with the No. 2 official at the Defense Department, Steve Feinberg, as NBC News reported this week. The FBI reviewed video showing Rush and Feinberg at a residence in the Washington region that is linked to the federal government, according to four people familiar with the video. Feinberg has been interviewed by the FBI, according to two people familiar with the investigation, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing, and the bureau said he is not under investigation. The CIA placed senior officials on leave after Rush’s arrest, NBC News reported. Rush allegedly lied to his employer about his background for nearly two decades. He had a high-ranking job in the spy agency, working on some of the most secret programs in the government. Federal agents seized about 300 gold bars at Rush’s home, federal officials alleged, along with about $2 million in U.S. currency and 35 luxury watches. Rush’s lawyer didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment. The lawyers in the case are under a protective order that bars them from sharing sensitive information in the case.

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Countdown is on as Senate races to pass crypto, college sports bills
articles.summary: Trump's Clarity Act faces a critical 60-vote test as Democrats demand crypto ethics rules tied to the President's $1.4 billion digital currency earnings.
articles.body: It’s a twofer in the Senate. Senators return to Washington Monday for the first time since the wee hours of Aug. 8. The Senate’s slated to meet for three weeks before heading home for the midterms — if the session even goes that long. There are a lot of items senators want to tackle. But only two big ones are lined up for test votes right now. The first legislative vote is locked in. It’s a procedural vote on a measure to regulate cryptocurrency. That comes Tuesday afternoon. The bill needs 60 votes to be in play. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: SUMMER ENDS, BUT THE SENATE'S FALL CRUNCH BEGINS There’s no bigger advocate for cryptocurrency than President Trump. He’s pushing for the Senate to move legislation. "We ended the war on crypto once and for all," said the President. "Now we need Congress to take the next step by passing the Clarity Act." Let’s clarify what the Clarity Act does. The measure clarifies federal rules for digital currencies and tokens. The framework would divide oversight between two regulators: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CTFC). Approval of the bill would be the first step toward establishing guardrails for cryptocurrency. "We passed the Clarity Act in the House last summer with 78 Democratic votes. It's now time for the Senate to join us," said House Financial Services Committee Chairman French Hill, R-Ark., on Fox Business. The package has bipartisan support. But there’s a roadblock coming from the Democrats. "The one remaining significant issue, I think, is the ethics provision," said Hill. President Trump’s own financial disclosure report reveals he earned $1.4 billion on cryptocurrency last year alone. That’s why Democrats want specific rules for the Trump family and crypto. "It basically exempts the President from any kind of ethical constraints. And that's just not going to fly in the Democratic caucus," said Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., says the bill is too closely aligned with what the President and his industry allies want. "Yes. We need crypto legislation. But not this legislation that has been written by this industry," said Warren. "I just don't see how anyone, Democrat or Republican, moves forward on this bill." That’s why many doubt the measure can score 60 votes twice to break a filibuster. The naysaying aggravates cryptocurrency advocates. "This is the right bill at the right time, and it's time to vote," said Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wy. She argues that crypto supporters bowed to demands to firm up ethics rules. "In 2023, we added 100 pages with stronger consumer protection provisions. Yet we got feedback from colleagues that they wanted more. So again, we listened. Today, this bill that was under 300 pages is more than 600 pages. That's hundreds of pages built over 11 months of daily bipartisan negotiations in windowless rooms where colleagues from both parties shared their priorities, and we worked diligently to incorporate them," said an exasperated Lummis. Warren argues that the bill makes it easier for drug runners and terrorists to fund their operations — without a literal paper trail. TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK Lummis says if the U.S. doesn’t establish its cryptocurrency blueprint, digital assets could flee overseas. "These companies can go to Singapore, Switzerland, the UAE and have a well-understood clear set of regulations," said Lummis. So that test vote is locked in. But it’s rare to pass a major financial regulatory measure this close to the midterms. And if Democrats prevail in November, that could create friction with the White House. The Senate also expects a test vote before the end of September on a bill to regulate money in college sports. But there’s no specific agreement on a date for that roll call tally. You know the old saying that there’s no such thing as bad publicity? Well, the "bad" publicity surrounding college football could potentially provide this legislation a boost. President Trump implored senators to stay in Washington to finish the bill last month. But it wasn’t ready. However, controversies over former pro players heading back to college — to say nothing of clock maintenance at the University of Michigan — could prod skeptical senators to give this measure another look. Let’s start with LSU tight end Dae’Quan Wright. If you can keep up with him. Last year, Wright played for current LSU head coach Lane Kiffin last year at Ole Miss — before Kiffin abandoned his squad late in the season for the Tigers. Wright decided to go pro. The Philadelphia Eagles picked him up in the spring. But then waved Wright early last month. The Cleveland Browns then signed Wright. He dressed for a preseason game against the Buffalo Bills. Never played a snap. Then the Browns cut him. So, Wright headed back to school. But this time, at LSU. "I’m just putting on a college uniform again and going out there and having fun and embracing my opportunity," said Wright. A judge then cleared Wright and former Ole Miss defensive lineman Zxavian Harris to play for LSU this fall. But in between, Harris appeared in preseason camp with the New Orleans Saints — before the team waived him. Drew Rosenhaus is Wright’s agent. He believes his client had no other option after his brief cup of coffee in the pros. "His contract with the NFL was terminated," said Rosenhaus. "If he was still able to play in the NFL, he would be there." Chaos like this is prodding lawmakers to try to regulate intercollegiate athletics. "It's not fair to the high school kids coming out to play college ball if you suddenly have colleges that are going and recruiting from the NFL," said Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas. Cruz teamed up with Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the Commerce panel, to craft the college athletics regulation measure. One big restriction: the legislation limits athletes to one transfer. "The transfer portal is out of control. You have athletes transferring two, three, four times. You have essentially no eligibility rules. So you have athletes competing six, seven, eight years. You have 28-year-olds competing against 17-year-old kids," said Cruz. The constant darting around from school to school worries the Trump administration, too. LAWMAKERS PRAISE BIPARTISAN EFFORTS LED BY TRUMP ADMIN TO ‘PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS’ "It's a crazy system, man," said Vice President JD Vance to colleague Lucas Tomlinson. "When I was growing up…you would get some loyalty, between the athletes and the fan bases. You would know the names of the people who played for your team because they were there for three or four years." The Cruz/Cantwell package also caps money schools can use for name, image and likeness, or NIL. And, considering the recent contretemps, the legislation bars athletes from going pro. Then reversing field to college. The White House tapped legendary former Alabama football coach Nick Saban to push for passage of the bill. "Join the winning team today and help Congress protect this American tradition," says Saban in the commercial now airing around the country. But even if the bill gets through the Senate, it faces an unclear path in the House. The House returns to session Monday, too. But it’s unclear how long its members will stick around with the midterms looming. "I've had coach Saban in my office, and we've talked about this, and he's right," said House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. "I think Congress is ready to act. But it takes both chambers." In other words, just like there’s a play clock in football, there’s a play clock in Congress, too. "I appreciate the exuberance of our Senate colleagues," said House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif. "But I don't know if there's enough days to get this done." articles.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board denounces ‘preposterous’ Trump dividend plan
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board on Thursday slammed President Trump’s proposal to dole out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if the GOP wins control in both chambers of Congress in November. The board noted in its opinion that the plan would amount to about $1.2 trillion when applied to the country’s roughly 240…
articles.body:
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board on Thursday slammed President Trump’s proposal to dole out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if the GOP wins control in both chambers of Congress in November.

The board noted in its opinion that the plan would amount to about $1.2 trillion when applied to the country’s roughly 240 million adult citizens.

“The amount is so preposterous that you’d almost think Mr. Trump is trying to show voters the absurdity of such income redistribution,” the board wrote.

The president debuted the controversial plan during his speech at the Republican National Committee’s convention in Dallas on Wednesday evening. He has not clarified where the money would be sourced.

“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump told the crowd.

The proposal drew immediate backlash, including from some Republicans. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) warned its implementation could “lead to more debt and inflation,” while former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) knocked it as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

The outlet’s editorial board accused the president of using the proposal to distract from discontent within the Republican Party around his administration’s tariffs on U.S. trade partners, like Canada and Mexico.

“Mr. Trump is resorting to this because voters are unhappy about inflation and don’t think his economic policies have helped them,” the board wrote. “His tariff tax increases are a big part of the reason. If he repealed those, he’d give the country an economic dividend without spending a dime.”

The U.S. imposed tariffs last month on a large swath of Canadian goods after the two countries failed to reach a new trade agreement. After Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs, Trump announced heightened tariffs on Canadian imports to go into effect early next year.

The president’s economic approval rating has also taken a hit during his administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil trading corridor, has driven up global energy rates.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: House to take up Russia sanctions bill next week

articles.body:
The House is set to take up legislation next week aimed at imposing tougher sanctions on Russia, after the measure cleared the Senate with overwhelming bipartisan support last month.

The House Rules Committee will meet Monday to consider the Russia sanctions bill, championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and backed by President Trump, along with other legislation. House GOP leaders are seeking to move the measure through regular order, meaning Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will need near-unanimous Republican support on a procedural vote to advance the bill on the floor.

It remains unclear whether Johnson has enough GOP votes to clear that hurdle, setting up a potential test for House Republicans before the chamber can take up the underlying legislation for final passage.

The measure could also face resistance from Democrats, who have bristled at giving Trump tariff authorities even if they want to find a way to provide additional U.S. support to Ukraine. They argue that the president already has ample authority to impose sanctions on companies, individuals and oil tankers financing Russia’s war machine.

Johnson told The Washington Examiner earlier this week at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas that “there should be bipartisan consensus” around the bill.

Margus Tsahkna, the minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Estonia, wrote on social platform X , “Estonia strongly supports imposing additional sanctions on Russia. We commend the U.S. Congress for their efforts and hope to see the Russian sanctions bill pass into law.”

If enacted, the measure would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and buyers of Russian oil and gas than the U.S. has previously enforced and extend existing sanctions on Iran, aiming to economically squeeze the two countries. The bill passed the Senate with broad bipartisan support last month.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), the lead Democratic sponsor of the measure, hailed it as a huge victory and recalled some of the final words he heard from Graham, the chief GOP sponsor, about the bill’s imminent passage.

“As he said to me in some of his last words, this is a big effing deal. We all did good,” he said. “A bipartisan team achieved this overwhelming 86-11 vote. President Zelensky is watching in Ukraine. President Putin is watching in Moscow,” he continued, referring to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: Cruz on $5K dividend: ‘I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working’
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), a prominent conservative voice in the Senate GOP conference, says he’s willing to support President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 dividend payments to U.S. adults provided that they are structured as tax refunds and go to people who work and pay taxes. Asked about Trump’s proposal, Cruz told Fox News’s Jesse…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), a prominent conservative voice in the Senate GOP conference, says he’s willing to support President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 dividend payments to U.S. adults provided that they are structured as tax refunds and go to people who work and pay taxes.

Asked about Trump’s proposal, Cruz told Fox News’s Jesse Watters that his support “depends on how it’s structured.”

“I would like to see it structured as a tax refund,” he said. “I would be all for structuring it as a tax refund.”

“But I think we should be incentivizing work. I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” he argued.

Trump unveiled the proposal at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas and has drawn pushback from both Republican moderates and conservatives.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) warned the idea would be “extraordinarily costly.”

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” she said in a statement.

Paying out a $5,000 dividend to nearly 270 million American adults would cost more than $1 trillion and add to the national debt, which recently passed the $40 trillion mark.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has defended the idea of putting money back in Americans’ pockets, but he hasn’t committed to voting on the proposal on the Senate floor.

Asked during a recent Fox News interview whether Senate Republicans would pass Trump’s proposal, Thune replied: “Well, that’s a good question.”

“We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it,” he said.

articles.body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s presence at Friday’s 9/11 remembrance at Ground Zero drew criticism from some in the city, including one former police officer who said the mayor "probably should have skipped it" and another mourner who called his appearance "disrespectful" and "very offensive." Mamdani has faced criticism over his associations with controversial political and online figures, as well as his decision to appoint Ramzi Kassem as his administration’s chief counsel. Kassem previously represented a Guantánamo detainee linked to an al Qaeda terrorist plot. Former New York Republican Gov. George Pataki, 9/11-era FDNY Commissioner Thomas von Essen and others called on Mamdani to skip the ceremony. "He showed up anyway. It does bother us," Walter Matuza, whose father Walter was killed that day, told Fox News Digital. MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY Matuza said he was part of the group of victims’ families that initiated the petition to keep Mamdani away. He cited Mamdani’s association with streamer Hasan Piker, who once said America "deserved 9/11," as well as Mamdani’s appointment of Kassem. MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER Matuza, of Staten Island, said his father was one of dozens at Carr Futures brokerage who died after American Airlines Flight 11 struck the north tower just above their 92nd floor offices. Mike, a former New Jersey police officer, told Fox News Digital he recalled watching the terror unfold on television from across the Hudson – and later came to Manhattan to help relieve exhausted NYPD officers stuck at their posts. "Based on the rhetoric that he's used in the past. Yeah, he probably should have skipped it," Mike said of Mamdani. He added that Mamdani’s appointment of Kassem also troubled him, saying the mayor could’ve handled the situation in a "whole different way." FAMILIES OF 9/11 VICTIMS' MESSAGE TO MAMDANI: 'PLEASE DO NOT COME' TO MEMORIAL CEREMONY "But, he did it and unfortunately people aren't going to forget it." Another mourner called Mamdani a "communist" when asked about his appearance on Friday, adding that the memorial was "not supposed to be a political event." Steven, who traveled all the way to New York from Hobe Sound, Florida, to attend the remembrance, lambasted Mamdani’s presence as "disrespectful" and "offensive." ZOHRAN MAMDANI URGED TO SKIP NEW YORK CITY'S 9/11 MEMORIAL: 'VILE ANTISEMITE' "I've been following that over the past couple weeks and I saw that I think they had upwards of 700,000 New Yorkers requesting him not to be here. I mean, as the mayor, I would assume he has the right to be here…. But who he represents and the people he's affiliated with… I feel that he should stay away. I don't feel that his presence here is wanted, and I think he should honor that as a human being." The petition had garnered more than 110,000 signatures at the time, according to the petition’s tally. Steven called Kassem’s appointment "hideous" and added that the youngest generation who does not remember or did not live through 9/11 are suffering from "incorrect information" and do not understand the reality of the terror attack. He said he will educate his children on 9/11 so that they do not go down the same ideological road. Attendee John told Fox News Digital that Mamdani does have a right to attend. John said he lost friends including at now-Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s Cantor-Fitzgerald firm – which lost more than 650 people; the most of any company in the Twin Towers that day – and that as long as Mamdani is respectful to the fallen Americans being remembered, he is "fine" with the Democrat attending. Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani for comment. In a prior statement, the mayor said he is proud of New York and "love[s] this city [and] country." "[W]hat I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers." During the ceremony, footage captured Mamdani approaching and greeting his 9/11-era predecessor, Republican Rudolph Giuliani. articles.body:
President Trump said Friday he’s “99 percent” sure he could have given a speech at the New York City 9/11 ceremony if he wanted to, while pushing back on reports that said he didn’t attend because he wouldn’t be able to give a speech.

“It’s just not true. I didn’t demand to speak,” he told Sid Rosenberg on 77 WABC on Friday.

“I’m sure if I wanted to speak, they would have let me,” he said, adding that he’s president and he knows “the guys down there.”

The New York Times reported last month that the president’s team told the organizers of New York City’s ceremony that he would like to speak. The National September 11 Memorial and Museum has banned speeches from politicians at the ceremony since 2012.

Trump joked that “I speak enough, the last thing I want to do is speak.”

“I don’t need it for any reason,” he said.

He singled out The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who was one of the reporters behind the report. The president railed against the report in a Truth Social post last month, calling it “Corrupt News.”

“I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a ‘solemn ceremony!’” he wrote.

Trump instead attended and gave remarks at the 9/11 ceremony at the Pentagon, while Vice President Vance attended the New York City memorial service.

Some presidents in the past visited all three sites — New York City; Arlington, Va., for the Pentagon; and Shanksville, Pa., for United Airlines Flight 93 — including former President Biden in 2021 for the 20th anniversary, former President Obama in 2011 for the 10th anniversary and former President George W. Bush on the first and fifth anniversaries.

articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday that the $5,000 dividends President Trump promised U.S. adults earlier this week would not come from taxpayer money.

In an interview with NBC News at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, Lutnick said, “It’s not tax money.”

“Together we’re going to deliver that plan and we’re going to pay that money to the Americans, and not from taxpayer money,” Lutnick continued.

Trump announced the dividends at the GOP’s midterm convention but said the money would only be given if Republicans maintained control of both chambers in Congress after November’s elections. The proposal would disburse a total of $1.2 trillion in dividends to roughly 270 million U.S. adults.

Lutnick said the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers.”

When asked where the money would come from, Lutnick cited the Trump Platinum Card — which is not launched yet — that would require immigration applicants to join a waitlist and allows for future applicants to live in the U.S. for 270 days per year without being subject to tax on non-U.S. income.

Applicants would have to pay a $15,000 processing fee, undergo Department of Homeland Security vetting and pay an additional $5 million contribution to the U.S. government to be guaranteed citizenship.

“We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” Lutnick said. “That’s $500 billion dollars.”

He also mentioned the investment the federal government made into Intel last year as another source of possible funds that Trump said generated more than $30 billion over the last several months.

“Everybody knows we got just about 500 million shares, and the stock was $20, and now it’s $100, so we’re up $50 billion,” Lutnick stated.

White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett also suggested Friday the funds could come from a reconciliation package .

The proposal has divided figures within the GOP: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was critical of the proposal, noting the rising national debt as a major drawback of the idea.

“What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another trillion-and-a-half dollars and then just try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation,” DeSantis said.

articles.title: At Ground Zero, 9/11 families turn to Trump as Obama’s old decision resurfaces
articles.summary: Terry Strada accused successive administrations of protecting Saudi Arabia and urged Trump to release unredacted 9/11 files on the 25th anniversary.
articles.body: On a cloudy morning at the site where two sprawling towers once stood, the loved ones of New Yorkers killed on 9/11 gathered with a message for President Donald Trump: Release the unredacted files they believe could implicate Saudi Arabia. Vice President JD Vance attended the ceremony alongside former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, as well as former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Gov. Andrew Cuomo were also among those in attendance. The message was delivered on the main stage by Terry Strada, whose husband, Tom, was killed in the attacks. Speaking from the memorial stage, Strada accused successive administrations of protecting Saudi Arabia instead of supporting the 9/11 families. Strada called out President Barack Obama, who was at the memorial, for vetoing the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, or JASTA, in 2016. Congress later overrode the veto, allowing 9/11 families to sue Saudi Arabia over its alleged role in the attacks. TRUMP SET TO HONOR 9/11 VICTIMS, FIRST RESPONDERS AT PENTAGON ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY "Administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," Strada said. "They withheld evidence. They vetoed JASTA. They broke promises, both public and private. It has been one betrayal after another. "President Trump can still change that" She urged the president to tell Saudi leaders "that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through." "Please carry that message back," another speaker said, addressing Vance. "Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors." The remarks drew applause from the crowd. "Administration after administration has not done anything for us. In fact, they've blocked, blocked us every step of the way of getting justice," Dennis McGinley, whose older brother Danny worked on the 89th floor of the South Tower, told Fox News Digital. "President Trump has a unique, historic opportunity here to be a hero, be our champion, finally close the books on this American nightmare, which is now becoming an American embarrassment. It's got to start." The appeal came as families marked the 25th anniversary of the attacks with a renewed push for accountability from Saudi Arabia, which they accuse of helping two of the hijackers establish themselves in the United States. The kingdom has repeatedly denied involvement. The families’ claims center on Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national who helped hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar obtain an apartment in San Diego, and Fahad al-Thumairy, an accredited Saudi diplomat and imam at the King Fahd Mosque in California who had numerous contacts with al-Bayoumi. The 9/11 Commission documented the men’s connections but did not conclude that the Saudi government or senior Saudi officials supported the plot. Its report also said investigators found no evidence that another Saudi national, Osama Bassnan, gave money to the hijackers. Newly released investigative material and evidence presented in a long-running civil case have intensified scrutiny of those connections. In August 2025, U.S. District Judge George Daniels allowed claims against Saudi Arabia to proceed, finding that the families had presented enough evidence to move toward trial. The ruling did not determine that Saudi Arabia was responsible for the attacks. The families say that legal ruling, along with additional FBI and British intelligence material, gives Trump an opportunity to release more records and help resolve what they view as a 25-year-old betrayal. SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’ For Passananti, the demand was inseparable from his own loss. His father, Horace Robert Passananti, was working on the 100th floor of the North Tower. Passananti was 32 when he called his father after hearing that a plane had struck the building. He never heard from him again. Passananti said he has attended the ceremony every year but one since the attacks. "I wish I wasn’t here, obviously, but I feel like I have to be here every year," he told Fox News Digital. Passananti, who is affiliated with the group 9/11 Justice, said families want those responsible for the attacks held accountable. "We’ve really been on our own — the families — trying to obtain evidence," Passananti said. "We’ve gotten really no help from our government. We feel like they’ve put Saudi Arabia ahead of the 9/11 families, and we’re hoping that will change." TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE He described the delays in the case as "a twilight zone." "It feels really like a twilight zone and unbelievable that we have to fight for justice for the worst terrorist attack that ever happened on our soil," Passananti said. "It doesn’t feel real. It’s unexplainable." Trump has previously acknowledged that questions remain unanswered about the attacks. In 2022, while defending his decision to host a Saudi-backed LIV Golf tournament at his New Jersey club amid protests from 9/11 families, Trump said, "Nobody has gotten to the bottom of 9/11." But Trump has not publicly said whether he supports releasing additional files concerning Saudi Arabia’s alleged ties to the hijackers. McGinley worked across the Hudson River and called his brother after seeing the first plane hit, believing it was a small aircraft. His brother told him it was a passenger jet and described seeing people jumping from the neighboring tower. McGinley asked Danny if he was evacuating, and he said he'd been told to remain in place just before the South Tower was hit. McGinley never spoke to him again. "It is like the wound never healed, and every year we get salt poured back into that wound," McGinley said. The families’ calls for answers extended beyond those killed on the day of the attacks. Relatives of first responders who later died from cancer and other illnesses linked to toxic exposure also gathered at the memorial to honor their loved ones. Jen Nilsen, whose husband died in the attacks, said the pain remains as strong as ever 25 years later. "It doesn’t change at the 25th year," Nilsen said. "The pain is still there." Nilsen said she returns to the memorial because "this is where he is." Her message to younger generations was simple. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Never forget," she said. "Even though years go on, you never forget. You never get over it. The hurt is always there. The pain is always here."

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: As Democrats protest in Dallas, conservatives are quiet and cautious
articles.summary: About 300 Democrats rallied at Dallas City Hall against Trump and the GOP, but quiet conservatives nearby tell a very different political story.
articles.body: On Thursday afternoon, former Democratic Party superstar Beto O’Rourke headlined a protest at Dallas City Hall that drew about 300 angry, loud Democrats and socialists convinced that in fighting against President Donald Trump and the GOP, they are saving America from fascism. At the entrance to the event was a man holding a sign that read "MAGA = Fascist," complete with a swastika on it. And that was one of the nicer sentiments expressed in the homage signage seen around the event. "I can’t stand the man. You cannot be a Christian while following that man," said Bonnie, an activist in her 60s, when asked why Trump provoked so much outright hatred. DAVID MARCUS: AHEAD OF GOP CONVENTION, DALLAS DEMS SHARE WORRIED OPTIMISM And it wasn’t just Trump. When asked about more generic Republicans like Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, or Sen. John Thune, R-N.D., Bonnie said, "If they allow him to do what he’s doing, they’re all in the same boat." Rick, also post-retirement age, held a sign that read, "Conservatives Against Trump," and described his values as "small, limited government, a strong national defense and fiscal responsibility." JOHN FETTERMAN DEFENDS TRUMP SUPPORTERS, CONDEMNS FELLOW DEMOCRATS' 'F--- TRUMP' STRATEGY Asked whether he was concerned that the leftward lurch of the Democrats also threatened those centrist principles, Rick replied, "Clearly, both parties, both major parties, have become polarized." From the stage came vitriol about everything from Jeffrey Epstein to data centers in the form of both speeches and song, while a small counterprotest was held at bay by Dallas police. The theme of fascism was present on so many of the signs that I eventually asked one protester what they meant by the term, to which he simply replied, "If you don’t know then I can’t help you," which was not particularly clarifying. The vocal zeal with which these protesters and other Democrats I met in Dallas denounce all things Republican stands in stark contrast with many of the conservatives I spoke to in the city, who, notwithstanding living in red Texas, tend to be a bit shy about their beliefs. "At my son’s school, and around some friends, I just don’t bring up that I support Trump. It's just not worth it," said one woman, who asked to remain anonymous. She also told me of friends she has who send out two sets of Christmas cards each year, one MAGA themed and one not. She now receives the former each holiday season. Another man, who works in the service industry, said, "I can’t tell anyone at work that I like Trump. So, when it comes up, I just say that I’m a Bill Maher-style centrist." At least in his mind, that is as far to the right as he can publicly be without it causing problems. It all reminded me of a young woman who I met last year who told me after we chatted that she didn’t know any conservatives and was surprised I was so nice. I asked her, "Do you have any guy friends who never ever talk about politics?" She said, "Yes," to which I replied, "Yeah, they’re conservative." BILL MAHER'S DIRE MIDTERM ELECTION WARNING TO DEMS AFTER 'REALLY CRAZY' SOCIALISTS WIN PRIMARIES I immediately felt a twinge of regret for outing them. When Ronald Reagan was winning elections, pundits described his supporters as a silent majority; today, what we have may be something closer to a silenced majority, as conservatives hide their identities to avoid conflict. This is a trend that I have discovered all across the country over the past few years: Praise of Trump seems always to come in a quiet whisper, criticism often loud enough for an entire room to hear. One has to wonder, at a time when polling consistently overestimates support for Democrats, if this shy Trump voter phenomenon might be in play. After all, people trained to keep quiet about their politics may not be eager to respond to polls. Many local Republican voters I spoke with are very nervous that this could be the year that Democrats finally flip Texas. But, in fairness, while they see myriad outward displays of affection for Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, they may have no idea that their friend supports GOP candidate Ken Paxton. The challenge for the Republican Party in this midterm cycle is to make sure that the Trump supporters who don’t want to admit it out loud will still show up to vote, making a difference despite their silence. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It is the quiet voters who are very likely to determine control of Congress, and whether the final two years of Trump’s presidency will be the solidification of his legacy or 24 long months of endless impeachment.

articles.title: AOC, Mamdani interaction caught on cam at 9/11 memorial sparks online fury
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were seen grinning at the 9/11 Memorial as a mourner sobbed nearby on camera.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., were lambasted Friday for appearing to share a moment of levity at the 9/11 Memorial in lower Manhattan during the solemn reading-of-the-names of victims. The Pittsburgh Republican Committee suggested on X that the sight was one of the reasons 9/11 victims families didn’t want the mayor there, while former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt also sounded off. ZOHRAN MAMDANI URGED TO SKIP NEW YORK CITY'S 9/11 MEMORIAL: 'VILE ANTISEMITE' "While normal Americans cry, commie Mamdani and AOC laugh it up at the 9/11 memorial in New York," Pratt said. A New York City lawmaker added that she was outraged to see Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez acting that way. "After thousands of families of victims of terror beg Mamdani not to show up, he stands there and laughs while families weep," said Councilwoman Inna Vernikov, R-Brighton Beach. articles.title: CIA warned of threat of 'explosive airplane' years before 9/11, documents show
articles.summary: The spy agency released 71 declassified presidential briefings, with one showing it had thought Al Qaeda's plans were 'widely known' by extremists.
articles.body:
Newly declassified documents show that three years before 9/11, US intelligence officials were discussing the possibility that al-Qaeda "may fly an explosive airplane into a US city".

On Friday, the 25th anniversary of hijacked planes being crashed into the World Trade Center, Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field, the CIA released 71 daily presidential briefs spanning from early 1998 to the day after the attacks.

Another document, dated 12 September 2001, said the plot's existence was "widely known" in extremist circles.

President's Daily Briefs are among the most secretive intelligence analyses in the US government, and typically remain classified for 40 or 50 years after publication.

"Twenty-five years ago, the 9/11 attacks struck a blow to our nation, but they did not break us," CIA Director John Ratlcliffe said in a statement

"Generations of C.I.A. officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring Al Qaeda would never again harm our country," he added.

Of the 71 documents published by the CIA, 69 have never been seen by the public.

The briefs - many still heavily redacted - were created during both the Clinton and Bush administrations.

They show increasing alarm over the al-Qaeda network and its leader, Osama Bin Laden. They also echo the assessment of the official commission that reviewed what happened that day that US intelligence repeatedly warned of a potential attack, but had few details or sense of the scale of what was coming.

One briefing document, dated 10 September 1998, reported Bin Laden's preferred location for a strike was within the US, with Washington a prime target.

The group, a CIA analyst wrote, "may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city".

While the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report noted US intelligence believed al-Qaeda was considering using an airplane in the attack, it was never clear that the warning reached then-President Bill Clinton.

Bin Laden and al-Qaeda were already well-known to the US intelligence community in1998.

In August that year, they attacked US embassies in both Kenya and Tanzania, killing 224 people and prompting the US to strike targets in Afghanistan and Sudan with cruise missiles.

One document written on 28 August 1998 - 21 days after the embassy attacks and eight days after the US retaliation - warned that the network remained intact and that Bin Laden was actively "considering attacks in the US".

Only one of the presidential briefings in the release comes from after the attacks. It was sent to the White House 0400 on 12 September, just under 20 hours from when the first aircraft struck the World Trade Center in New York.

The report noted that "mounting evidence" suggested extremists in Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf "were aware" the attack had been imminent.

Another partially redacted sentence said the plot was "widely known" among extremists and that Bin Laden may have relocated to Kabul, in Afghanistan, to avoid conflict with the country's Taliban rulers with whom he had "clashed" over the plan.

The then-head of the Taliban, Mullah Omar, was reported to have been evacuated with his family from the southern Afghan city of Kandahar immediately following the attacks. Less than a month later, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan, seeking to destroy al-Qaeda.

articles.title: Inside Trump’s intimate meeting with nation’s bravest soldiers during whirlwind Texas trip
articles.summary: Trump toured the new National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, then signed legislation for a new monument near the Lincoln Memorial.
articles.body: ARLINGTON, Texas — During his whirlwind trip to Texas to rally Republican voters ahead of November’s elections, President Donald Trump on Thursday made a pit stop to honor America’s bravest warriors the day before the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The intimate gathering was held at the National Medal of Honor Museum, where Trump also met privately with the Medal of Honor recipients who were present. Trump also signed legislation clearing the way for a new monument honoring the award's recipients on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., before addressing roughly 100 guests, including 16 of the nation’s 65 living Medal of Honor recipients. REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG "It’s very special for all of us," Trump said. "It's special for me to be here, and it's an American treasure devoted to the best and bravest warriors of our country. And, frankly, it's really the best they've ever produced." The event was a stark contrast to the tens of thousands to whom Trump had addressed about 13 hours prior at the GOP midterm convention, a half hour away in Dallas. DAVID MARCUS: IN DALLAS, GOP SEEKS UNITY ON 9/11, KIRK ANNIVERSARIES Charlotte Jones, daughter of Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, is the chairman of the museum’s board of directors and served as the event’s emcee. Her father beamed with pride as he sat front and center, which Trump noted from the stage. High-ranking Republican politicians, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, were among the high-profile guests who huddled in the room for the event. Both Jones and Troy Bertram, the CEO of the new center, stressed that the National Medal of Honor Museum (NMOH) is not just a war museum. "We are not a military history museum," Bertram told Fox News Digital. "We are storytelling around the humans, about their courage, their sacrifice. Who they were before what they became." Trump’s speech struck a tone of admiration for the men and women honored by the museum. MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH' "They stormed into hellfire and crushed America's enemies," the president said. "They had bravery like few people could even think of having. They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs and carried them back and forth. … They stood in the way of bullets, purposely just standing just like this and taking bullets, and it's amazing." One of those warriors was Army Lt. Col. William Swenson, a man of steely resolve who serves on the museum’s board. DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL His heroic 2009 actions in Afghanistan, where he fought during Operation Enduring Freedom, earned him the highest military decoration awarded by the U.S. government in 2013, presented by then-President Barack Obama. Pinned down by the enemy during a seven-hour battle in the Ganjgal Valley of the country’s Kunar Province, Swenson saved lives by making multiple trips into active combat zones, pulling wounded soldiers to safety and loading them onto helicopters for evacuation. "The president and our commander-in-chief has been a strong supporter of this project," Swenson told Fox News Digital. "He continues to be a strong supporter of this project, and having him as involved as he is going to be a great contribution to get the monument done to standard, on time and to start signaling the messaging to the American people what’s important about service." The 47th president is working with private donors to build the new monument in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, in honor of recipients of the nation’s highest military award for heroism in battle. He previously signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act, officially clearing the path for its construction. WWII VET GIVES DIRECT MESSAGE TO YOUNG PEOPLE TODAY: 'WE GAVE UP OUR YESTERDAYS FOR YOUR TOMORROWS' "When he died, Woody was the last surviving recipient from World War II. [He] had one of the most dangerous jobs of war, and that’s operating a flamethrower," Trump said, speaking of the man for whom the bill was named. "In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory — literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gauntlet of enemy strongholds. And back and forth he went. He just kept going back and forth." Williams was one of about 300 flamethrowers in Iwo Jima, a famed and defining battle in the war’s Pacific theater. The late soldier’s family members were in the audience and were fondly acknowledged by the president. "America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked [and] what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country," Trump concluded. "I want to thank you all once again." Swenson described the importance of remembrance. "What we do to ensure that we have common history, common beliefs, is we have monuments, and we have museums. We have our mythology that tells us who we are as Americans and what we will continue to be in the future," he said. "Without this mythology, we don’t have that narrative. The fact that the event was held the day before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 wasn’t lost on him, either. He described the tragedy as a "seminal event" for him, which happened just as he was finishing college, that shaped his entire future. Swenson spent 22 years in the Army after the attack. "The United States is forged in fire," he said. "We’ve had revolutions, we’ve had civil wars, we’ve had global conflicts, we’ve had civil strife. There will always be challenges to our freedom and to our country, and it’s up to us to move forward from those events and create that more perfect union. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "That said, we must always learn from these events to help better prevent them and also to honor the sacrifice of the service members who fought in these conflicts, and also understand how we as citizens can create a better country that does not have these problems — that does not have these challenges. It’s our responsibility to future generations to prevent that."

articles.title: Democrats shift their mail voting message: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jane C. Timm and Natasha Korecki explore how Democrats are pushing early and in-person voting amid mail ballot concerns. Plus, Kristen Welker examines whether the GOP’s midterm convention can help the party solve a key dilemma this fall. — Adam Wollner Democrats shift their mail voting message By Jane C. Timm and Natasha Korecki Democrats and progressive groups are urging voters to cast their ballots as early as possible — and increasingly, in person — amid concerns that President Donald Trump’s intervention and postal delays could disrupt the mail voting process this fall. Less than eight weeks from Election Day, the legal fate of an executive order from Trump that would restrict mail voting remains unclear, with a ruling from the Supreme Court over whether it can be implemented expected soon. Aside from the order, budget issues and operational changes to the U.S. Postal Service have slowed mail delivery. Since the Covid pandemic, Democrats in particular have championed mail voting, which their voters have relied on more than Republicans’ in recent elections. But ahead of the midterms, with control of the House and Senate up for grabs, they have pumped the brakes on that message. “State parties traditionally really pushed two key messages when it came to voting: Vote on Election Day or vote by mail. And when we talked about voting by mail, it was, ‘Get your ballot back by Election Day,’” said Jane Kleeb, who chairs the Association of State Democratic Committees and serves as a Democratic National Committee vice chair. “This time around, we are really pushing people … to say, ‘Vote early in person. Go to your county election office and vote early in person.’ And that this is the best way that we can get Democrats elected is if you vote early in person.” While Democrats are putting a greater emphasis on in-person voting this year, they aren’t discouraging voters if they want to cast a ballot by mail. Rather, Kleeb said the party will stress that they need to put their ballots in the mail or a drop box well before Election Day. “We say that we still believe that voting by mail is safe and secure,” she said. “This election cycle in particular, you need to give an extra week for your ballot to arrive in time.” Read more → Can the midterm convention rally Trump’s base? Analysis by Kristen Welker With their midterm convention in Dallas this week, Republicans attempted to confront one of their biggest dilemmas heading into November: how to fire up President Donald Trump’s loyal base when he’s not on the ballot. “Pretend that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the crowd Wednesday night. On Thursday night, Trump had attendees raise their hands and “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States” that “on Nov. 3 we are going to go out and vote.” As part of his pitch, Trump said that the government would pay each adult American a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate, though there are major questions around how such a plan would work. Trump and other Republican speakers at the convention also cast Democrats as extreme and out of touch, often labeling them communists. It does raise the question of whether Republicans are failing to appreciate the energy on the left, which has fueled progressive victories and sky-high turnout in primaries this year. Turning out the president’s supporters could be key to holding on to the Senate, given that states like Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Ohio that Trump won by double digits in 2024 could decide the majority. But Republicans will also need to appeal to independents and moderate voters in crucial swing states like Michigan and North Carolina. And the GOP still faces significant headwinds heading into November, even among Trump’s most ardent supporters. While Republicans still broadly support the president, the share who “strongly approve” of his job performance has dropped 11 points since the spring to 41%, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. Trump’s overall job approval among Americans is at 36%. That’s in line with a new Quinnipiac University poll of registered voters that showed Trump’s job approval at 33% and Democrats with an 11-point lead in the battle for Congress. The GOP’s struggles come amid widespread opposition to the Iran war and concerns about the cost of living, particularly high gas prices, including among Republicans. Vice President JD Vance acknowledged those concerns during his convention speech Thursday, imploring supporters, “Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater.” He added, “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.” Trump also acknowledged this week for the first time that he does not expect the Iran war to end or for gas prices to come down before the midterms. So while the president may have fired up his supporters in Dallas, the bigger test will come when voters head to the polls in 53 days. We’ll discuss the fight ahead in the midterms on “Meet the Press” this Sunday with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. I’ll also speak with Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who sounded the alarm about the threats from artificial intelligence. 🎈More from the convention: Republicans attempted to address voters’ economic concerns, with speakers mentioning themes of affordability, prices and costs at least 178 times, according to an analysis by NBC News. On the other hand, the Iran war was largely ignored. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
